questions.prompt: What happens when a mutable object is used as a default argument value?

options.text: It is created once and shared across every call
It is recreated fresh on each call
Python raises a SyntaxError
It is silently converted to a tuple

questions.explanation: Default arguments are evaluated once at function definition. A default empty list therefore accumulates across calls, which is why None is used as the sentinel instead.

questions.prompt: What does the Global Interpreter Lock actually prevent?

options.text: Any use of threads at all
Two threads executing Python bytecode simultaneously
Multiple processes running in parallel
Async code from running concurrently

questions.explanation: Only one thread runs bytecode at a time, so threads do not speed up CPU-bound work. They still help with I/O-bound work, because the lock is released while waiting.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of a generator over building a list?

options.text: It can be indexed randomly
It sorts its output automatically
It can be iterated many times
It yields items lazily instead of holding them all in memory

questions.explanation: A generator produces values on demand, so a ten-million-row file streams in constant memory. The trade-off is that it is single-pass and cannot be indexed.

questions.prompt: In Python, what does a decorator do?

options.text: Wraps a function to extend or alter its behaviour
Adds type annotations at runtime
Marks a function for garbage collection
Compiles a function to C

questions.explanation: A decorator takes a function and returns a replacement, which is how logging, caching and route registration are added without editing the function body.

questions.prompt: Why should a virtual environment be used per project?

options.text: It makes imports resolve faster
It isolates dependency versions between projects
It is required to run Python 3
It encrypts installed packages

questions.explanation: Two projects often need different versions of the same library. Without isolation, installing one breaks the other, and system Python gets polluted besides.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a list and a tuple?

options.text: Tuples can only hold numbers
Lists cannot be nested
Tuples are immutable and can be dictionary keys
Lists are always faster to iterate

questions.explanation: Immutability makes a tuple hashable, so it can be a dict key or set member. It also signals that the collection is a fixed record rather than a growable sequence.

questions.prompt: In Django, what does an ORM queryset's laziness mean?

options.text: Queries are cached for the whole process lifetime
Queries run only when the result is actually needed
Queries always run on a background thread
Queries are limited to 100 rows by default

questions.explanation: Building a queryset issues no SQL; iterating, slicing or calling len does. This is what allows filters to be chained and composed before a single query is sent.

questions.prompt: What does select_related do in Django?

options.text: Restricts which columns are returned
Caches the queryset in Redis
Filters rows by a related field
Follows foreign keys with a SQL join in the same query

questions.explanation: It joins forward relations up front, avoiding a query per row when the template touches a related object. prefetch_related handles many-to-many with a second query instead.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the if __name__ == '__main__' guard?

options.text: It runs the block only when the file is executed directly
It prevents the module from being imported
It declares the entry point required by Python
It makes the module thread-safe

questions.explanation: On import, __name__ is the module name, so the block is skipped. Without it, importing a script runs its side effects, which also breaks multiprocessing on some platforms.

questions.prompt: What does a context manager, used via with, guarantee?

options.text: The block runs in a separate scope
Cleanup runs even if the block raises
The block is retried on failure
Variables inside are automatically typed

questions.explanation: __exit__ runs on both the normal and exceptional path, which is why with open(...) reliably closes a file where a bare close call would be skipped by an exception.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy?

options.text: A deep copy is always faster
A shallow copy cannot copy lists
A shallow copy shares nested objects; a deep copy duplicates them
They differ only for immutable objects

questions.explanation: A shallow copy duplicates the outer container only, so mutating a nested list is visible through both copies. deepcopy recurses, at the cost of time and memory.

questions.prompt: When does asyncio actually improve throughput?

options.text: For CPU-bound numeric loops
For I/O-bound work with many concurrent waits
For any code, since it uses all cores
Only when combined with threads

questions.explanation: Async gives concurrency, not parallelism. It shines when most time is spent waiting on the network or disk; a tight CPU loop just blocks the event loop.

questions.prompt: What does *args allow in a function signature?

options.text: Accepting any number of positional arguments as a tuple
Accepting keyword arguments as a dict
Forcing all arguments to be keyword-only
Declaring the argument types

questions.explanation: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple; **kwargs collects keyword arguments into a dict. The names are convention, the stars are what matter.

questions.prompt: Why is a list comprehension usually preferred over an equivalent for loop with append?

options.text: It runs on multiple cores
It uses no memory
It can iterate infinite sequences
It is more concise and somewhat faster

questions.explanation: The comprehension avoids repeated attribute lookup and method calls, and states intent in one line. Once it needs several clauses, a loop is more readable again.

questions.prompt: What is duck typing in Python?

options.text: Compile-time type checking of annotations
Suitability is determined by available methods, not declared type
Automatic conversion between numeric types
Restricting a function to one argument type

questions.explanation: If an object supports the operations used, it works, regardless of its class. This is why a file-like object with a read method can stand in for a real file.

questions.prompt: What do type hints do at runtime by default?

options.text: They raise TypeError on a mismatch
They coerce values to the annotated type
Nothing; they are checked by external tools
They speed up attribute lookup

questions.explanation: CPython stores annotations and ignores them. Enforcement comes from mypy or pyright, or from a library like Pydantic that reads them deliberately.

questions.prompt: In Flask or FastAPI, why is a global mutable variable a poor place for per-user state?

options.text: Globals are read-only in Python
It is shared across all requests and workers diverge
Globals are cleared after every request
It prevents the app from starting

questions.explanation: One process serves many requests, so a global leaks one user's data into another's. With several worker processes, each also holds a different copy.

questions.prompt: What does pip freeze produce?

options.text: A list of installed packages with exact versions
A frozen executable of the application
A lock preventing further installs
A cache of downloaded wheels

questions.explanation: It snapshots the environment so a build elsewhere resolves to the same versions. It also captures transitive dependencies, which is why a curated requirements file is often kept separately.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between is and == in Python?

options.text: is compares values; == compares identity
They are interchangeable for all types
is compares object identity; == compares value
== only works on numbers

questions.explanation: is asks whether two names point at the same object. Small integers and short strings are interned, so is sometimes appears to work on values, which makes the bug intermittent.

questions.prompt: Why does catching a bare except: hide bugs?

options.text: It is a syntax error in Python 3
It catches everything, including KeyboardInterrupt and typos
It suppresses only ValueError
It prevents the finally block from running

questions.explanation: A bare except swallows every exception, including programming errors like a misspelled attribute, so failures become silent. Catch the specific exception you can handle.

questions.prompt: What does a dictionary comprehension's key collision do?

options.text: Raises a KeyError
Keeps the first value seen
Stores both values in a list
Keeps the last value seen

questions.explanation: Later assignments overwrite earlier ones silently. Building a dict keyed on a non-unique field therefore loses rows without any error, which is a common data bug.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of __init__.py in a package directory?

options.text: It marks the directory as a package and runs on import
It is the entry point executed by python -m
It lists the package's dependencies
It is required for every Python file to import

questions.explanation: It makes the directory a regular package and is executed on first import, which is where a package's public names are commonly re-exported.

questions.prompt: Why can a Python set not contain a list?

options.text: Sets only accept strings and numbers
Lists are unhashable because they are mutable
Lists are too large to store in a set
Sets require ordered elements

questions.explanation: Set membership relies on a stable hash. A mutable object's hash could change after insertion, so lists are deliberately unhashable while tuples are not.

questions.prompt: What does the Django migration system track?

options.text: Data changes made through the admin
Which URLs have been registered
Ordered schema changes derived from model edits
Deployment history of the application

questions.explanation: makemigrations diffs models against the last migration and writes an ordered, dependency-aware change file, so every environment reaches the same schema.

questions.prompt: Why is string concatenation in a large loop discouraged in Python?

options.text: Strings cannot exceed a fixed length
The interpreter forbids it above 1000 iterations
It converts the result to bytes
Strings are immutable, so each step allocates a new object

questions.explanation: Every concatenation copies the accumulated string, giving quadratic behaviour. Collecting parts in a list and calling join allocates once.
